title: 28 Investigating bovine blood bacterial populations through 16S V4 sequencing, dPCR, and qPCR with specific focus on Hemotrophic Mycoplasma Wenyonii
content:
Abstract
Microbiomes have become an increasingly intense field of study over the last decade. Data has emerged to support the idea that microbes play important roles in disease control, metabolic efficiency, and more. Microbial DNA is detectable outside of the digestive tract in tissues such as blood. Multiple blood-borne pathogens such as hemotrophic Mycoplasma are widely endemic in cattle populations globally with most research focusing on dairy cattle. Hemoplasma are thought to be responsible for reducing male fertility and milk production, and yet the burden of infection is not well understood in beef cattle. Multiple strains of M. wenyonii have been identified, including the Massachusetts strain and the INFAP01 strain. These diverse strains may be confounding detection attempts through conventional testing methods. Furthermore, coinfection of multiple hemotrophic species is a likely contributor to disease progression from latent infection to acute disease. To investigate the diversity of microbial DNA present in blood, as well quantify the presence of known erythrocytic species M. wenyonii, blood was taken from 120 Texas beef cattle, located in Erath County. Blood was collected from 61 cows, 55 calves, and 4 bulls. DNA extraction was performed and underwent library preparation of the 16S locus. DNA extractions were also utilized for both qPCR and dPCR to quantify the presence of M. wenyonii using two different probe binding sites to separate the INFAP01 strain from the broader M. wenyonii species. After rarefaction, ASVs were visualized in MicrobiomeAnalyst Marker Data Profiling, separated into the following groups for analysis: Adult female cows (n=61), adult male bulls (n=4), juvenile male calves (n=27), juvenile female calves (n=28). Statistical analysis was performed in QIIME 1.9 and R Studio, including differential abundance, Spearman rank correlation, and Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA. At the prokaryotic phylum level, significant differences were seen for Acidobacteria between males and females (p < 0.001). For genera associated with erythrocytic parasitism, relative abundance differed between juveniles and adults, with adults having a greater proportion of Bartonella and Mycoplasma (p < 0.001). Frequency of broad M. wenyonii infection was greater among adult females compared to calves (p = 0.006). These data suggest that there is a considerable presence of erythrocytic organisms in the blood of apparently healthy cattle and that levels differ across age groups. Additionally, there is evidence of diverse bacterial DNA present in bovine blood, but further work is needed to determine the source and viability of a functional bacterial presence.
